content.chapter: Chapter 1: The City and the Age
objectives: Describe who led Mecca and who suffered there, using the chapter’s own sentences as evidence.
Explain why the period was called the Age of Ignorance (Jahiliyyah) as the chapter does, without reducing it to “people could not read”.
Discover how “For this reason” points back to a reason, how because and while link ideas, and why the chapter uses the passive and “describes … as …”.
Propose one fair rule that would protect a vulnerable group today.
content.pedagogy: Build a simple power pyramid on the board from the text: Rich merchants at the top, powerful people below them, poor and weak people at the bottom, each level with a quoted phrase. Grammar grows out of meaning: You ask “Why was Mecca called the Republic of Merchants? Where is the answer?” and learners find that it is the sentence before “For this reason”, so they discover what “this reason” points to before you name the pattern. The passive is noticed the same way: “Who suffered? Who treated them badly? Why doesn’t the writer say?”
priorKnowledge: Past simple of be; because; basic words for social groups (rich, poor, leader, tribe, merchant).
anticipatedMisconceptions: Jahiliyyah is not presented as illiteracy: The chapter links the name to religious and social disorder.
The chapter does not say that every person in Mecca was cruel; it describes who held power, unfair treatment and common violence.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: For this reason pointing back to a reason · because + subject + verb for a reason · while for two situations side by side (contrast) · passive were … treated to keep the people affected in focus · X describes Y as Z to name the source of a description.
Notice (Activity 1): Board “Before Islam, Mecca was led by a council of rich merchants. For this reason, the city was known as the Republic of Merchants.” Ask only: “Why did people call Mecca the Republic of Merchants? Where is the answer?” Learners draw an arrow from “this reason” back to the first sentence and say the rule in their own words before the app confirms it.
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete the lines with because / while and explain why because of / during do not fit, then rewrite “people from poor backgrounds were often treated badly” in the active and “The Qur’an describes this period as …” in the passive. Ask: “Which version keeps the poor people first? Why does the writer prefer it?”
Likely errors: *because of religious and social disorder was common · *were often treat badly · *describes this period like a time of … · reason and result reversed around “For this reason”.
Use (Activity 4): a 5–6 sentence historical snapshot of another city or society with one reason, one while-contrast and one “was called / is described as”.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the key sentence: “beFORE ISlam, | MECca was LED | by a COUNcil of rich MERchants.” Then a clear pause after “For this REAson, |”.
Contrastive stress on the two groups: “POWerful people controlled many parts of life, | while POOR and WEAK people lived in MISery.”
Weak forms in the passive: “were OFten TREATed BADly” — “were” is /wə/.
Word focus: cha-OT-ic (/keɪ/), MIS-er-y, CRU-el-ty, VI-o-lence, re-LI-gious, GOV-ern-ment.
beforeReading: Ask: “If there is no government and no police, who protects a poor family?” Pairs give one answer. Keep three answers on the board as hypotheses to check in the text.
duringReading: First listening, books closed: Who led Mecca?
Build the power pyramid: One quoted phrase for each level.
Underline the reason for the name “Age of Ignorance”.
Circle “For this reason” and draw an arrow to the reason it points back to.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the pyramid in view.
Language Focus: Discover what “this reason” points to (Activity 1), then complete because / while and rewrite the passive and “describes … as …” (Activities 2–3).
Write a 5–6 sentence snapshot of another historical city or society (Activity 4).
Suggest one fair rule that would protect a weak group in your school or town.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “No government, no police — who protects a poor family?” pairs answer, three hypotheses stay on the board; 4–12 Listen with books closed (Who led Mecca?), then read along; 12–19 Power pyramid in pairs: Rich merchants / powerful people / poor and weak people, each level with a quoted phrase, then a quick whole-class check against the hypotheses; 19–23 Quick Challenge individually; 23–32 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Why “Republic of Merchants”? Where is the reason?), Activities 2–3 in pairs while you listen for because / because of; 32–38 Use: Learners draft a snapshot of another city or society they know from history lessons, two volunteers read and the class names the reason and the contrast; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Who held power in Mecca before Islam, and what is the evidence?
Why was the period called the Age of Ignorance, according to the chapter?
Why does the chapter say “were often treated badly” instead of naming who treated them badly?
interactiveTips: Open the Republic of Merchants hotspot only after learners have found the reason for the name themselves.
Use the Mecca hotspot to establish time and place, not to add social details.
Replay the while-sentence: Learners raise one hand when they hear the powerful and two hands when they hear the poor and weak.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the pyramid with the three labels already written and the frames “Mecca was led by ____. For this reason, ____.” and “____ controlled many parts of life, while ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six connected sentences about another society using because, for this reason, while, one passive sentence and one “is described as”.

formativeAssessment: Identifies who led and who suffered with quoted evidence.
Explains what “this reason” refers to.
Uses because + clause and while correctly and explains why the passive is used.
expectedResponses: Mecca was led by a council of rich merchants, so it was known as the Republic of Merchants; powerful people controlled many parts of life while poor and weak people lived in misery and were often treated badly.
content.transferTask: Propose one fair rule that would protect a weak group in your school or town, and say who would benefit.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover what “this reason” points back to before I explained it, and did they explain the passive by who is in focus?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, draw a power pyramid with three levels: rich merchants, powerful people, poor and weak people. Put a quoted phrase on each level.
checkQuestions: How many levels? (three)
What goes on each level? (a quoted phrase)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check the pyramid against the three hypotheses from the hook. In Activities 2–3, listen for because and because of. Ask why the passive “were often treated badly” leaves out the doer.

exitTicket: Write one “For this reason, …” sentence and one “while” sentence about a place you know.

interculturalFocus.notice: The chapter describes who led Mecca and who suffered, and the period called the Jahiliyyah.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which English words describe a society where the strong rule and the weak suffer ('injustice', 'inequality')? Can you find an example of this in the history of another country (for example, serfs in medieval Europe)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: The chapter says 'were often treated badly', not 'everyone treated them badly'. Learners keep this careful language and avoid judging a whole people.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write key words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain in three sentences why life was hard before Islam. The partner checks one detail in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 2 and B reads paragraph 3. Each explains the main idea to the partner without looking. The partner asks one question.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads paragraph 2 aloud. Asker asks “Why was Mecca called the Republic of Merchants?”. Writer notes the answer. Change roles for paragraph 3.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: An exchange student asks, “What makes a society fair?” The learner gives two ideas and compares them with old Mecca.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “There was no central government in Arabia, and tribes were the basis of society.” into their home language. How did each pair render “the basis of”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why the time before Islam was called the Age of Ignorance. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The writer explains the name Jahiliyyah in the first paragraph. Why start the book with a name?” (The whole book explains this name.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give the meaning of Jahiliyyah. The notes keep the rich and the poor apart.

objectives: Build the chapter’s definition of the Jahiliyyah from its stated features: People did not truly know Allah, and many did not have justice, order and peace.
Explain why the writer must first talk about Mecca, and name three facts that make Mecca important in the chapter.
Discover how the writer organises an explanation (To understand …, we must first …, this city), use describe + thing + as …, move a when-clause and insert a definition between commas.
Write a short explanatory profile of an important place.
content.pedagogy: Treat the chapter as a model of explaining. Learners first collect the features of the Jahiliyyah in a definition box and list what makes Mecca important (the House of Allah, the Prophet’s birthplace, the Qiblah). The language grows from one question, “How does the writer move from the period to the city?”: pairs order the sentences on paper strips and discover that “To understand …, we must first …” announces the plan and that “this city” can only come after Mecca has been named.
priorKnowledge: The difference between a definition and an example; simple when-clauses; Chapter 1 (Jahiliyyah).
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Jahiliyyah is not defined as “people knew nothing”; the chapter names specific things that were missing.
The chapter defines the Qiblah as a direction Muslims face during salah, not as a building.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: explanation order (To understand …, we must first …; this city pointing back) · describe + thing + as + description (described Islam as the opposite of barbarism) · a when-clause before or after the main clause · a definition inserted between commas (The Qiblah, the direction Muslims face during salah, …).
Notice (Activity 1): pairs put four sentences in order, then answer: “Which sentence tells us the plan of the explanation? Which words can only come after Mecca has been named?”
Build (Activities 2–3): rebuild “Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) described Islam as the opposite of barbarism.”, then move the when-clause to the front with a comma and unpack the inserted definition of the Qiblah.
Likely errors: *described Islam like the opposite · a fronted when-clause without a comma · “this city” used before the city is named · the inserted definition left without its second comma.
Use (Activity 4): a 5–6 sentence explanatory profile of another city, place or institution with “To understand …, we must first …” and one inserted definition.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Read the plan sentence in two chunks: “To underSTAND the Jahiliyyah PERiod, | we must FIRST talk about MECca.”
Inserted definition: lower the voice and speed up a little between the pauses: “The QIBlah, | the diRECtion Muslims FACE during SAlah, | is ALso located in MECca.”
Date: “in six ten C E”.
Word focus: BAR-ba-rism, rev-e-LA-tion, OP-po-site, lo-CA-tion, di-REC-tion.
beforeReading: Write on the board: “A fair definition = features + evidence, not a slogan.” Ask pairs what they would need to know to define a period of history. Collect two ideas.
duringReading: Box the definition sentence and list the features that follow it.
Circle the sentence that tells us the plan of the explanation.
Number three facts that make Mecca important.
Underline the definition of the Qiblah between commas.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge using the definition box.
Language Focus: Order the explanation (Activity 1), rebuild the “described … as …” sentence (Activity 2), then move the when-clause and unpack the inserted definition (Activity 3).
Write a 5–6 sentence profile of another important place with one inserted definition (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Warm-up: “features + evidence, not a slogan”, pairs list what a fair definition of a period needs; 4–12 Listen for gist (When did this era end?), then read and box the definition; 12–18 Definition box and Mecca list in pairs: Features of the Jahiliyyah / three facts about Mecca, each with a quoted phrase; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 first with four paper strips on the desk (pairs explain which words forced the order), then on screen, Activities 2–3 in pairs; 31–38 Use: Learners write a profile of their town, school or a famous building starting “To understand ____, we must first …” with one definition between commas, partners check both commas; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which features does the chapter use to define the Jahiliyyah?
Why does the writer say “we must first talk about Mecca”?
What does the description of Islam as “the opposite of barbarism” tell us about how the chapter sees the period?
interactiveTips: Use the Revelation hotspot to confirm when the era ended (610 CE).
Use The Holy Ka’ba hotspot for the sentence about Allah choosing the city as the location of His House.
Replay the Qiblah sentence and ask learners to tap the desk at each comma.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frame “The Jahiliyyah was ____. People did not ____, and many people did not have ____.” and a three-line list for Mecca with the first words given (Allah chose …, Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) was …, The Qiblah …).
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a six-sentence profile with “To understand …, we must first …”, one “describe … as” sentence, one fronted when-clause and one inserted definition.

formativeAssessment: Builds the definition from the chapter’s features.
Explains how “To understand …” and “this city” hold the explanation together.
Places “as” correctly and punctuates the fronted when-clause and the inserted definition.
expectedResponses: The Jahiliyyah was an age of barbarism in which people did not truly know Allah and many did not have justice, order and peace; it ended when the first revelation began in 610 CE, and it is explained through Mecca, the city of the Ka’ba, the Prophet’s birthplace and the location of the Qiblah.
content.transferTask: Define one place that matters to your community in two sentences: One definition and one fact inserted between commas.
content.teacherReflection: Did the strip ordering help learners see how an explanation is built, and did they keep the definition as precise as the chapter?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, fill the definition box with the features of the Jahiliyyah, and the Mecca list with three facts. Add a quoted phrase to each item.
checkQuestions: What goes in the definition box? (the features)
How many facts about Mecca? (three)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Start Activity 1 with paper strips and ask which words forced the order. Check that the definition uses the chapter’s features, not a slogan. In the Use task, check the commas around the inserted definition.

exitTicket: Complete “To understand ____, we must first ____.” and write one sentence with a definition between commas.

rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the boxed definition.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains how “To understand …” and “this city” hold the explanation together.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What does this city refer to?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses describe … as, a fronted when-clause and an inserted definition.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one model of each.

rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “To understand …, we must first …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The writer defines the Jahiliyyah and explains why we must first talk about Mecca. Some periods have special names in different cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which names for historical periods do you know in Turkish (Lale Devri, Tanzimat) and in English history (the Victorian era, the Dark Ages)? What does each name tell you about how later people saw that time?
interculturalFocus.perspective: A period's name is often given later and shows a viewpoint. Learners notice who named the period and why.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note what Jahiliyyah was and why Mecca matters.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners give three reasons why Mecca is important for Muslims.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner tells a partner how Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) described Islam. The partner says what the opposite was.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Finder finds the sentence about 610 CE. Reader reads it aloud. Explainer says what began then.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “Which direction do Muslims face when they pray, and why?” The learner answers with the chapter.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Mecca is the holy city of Islam.” into their home language. Which word did each pair choose for “holy”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why Mecca is the holy city of Islam. Next lesson ask what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The writer says ‘To understand the Jahiliyyah period, we must first talk about Mecca.’ What does this sentence do?” (It tells the reader what comes next.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give three reasons. The notes give the year 610 CE.

objectives: Put the beginning of Mecca in order: Abraham (pbuh) brings Ishmael (pbuh) and Hagar → Zamzam is discovered → the Jurhumites settle → the Ka’ba is built again → it becomes a pilgrimage site → the city grows rapidly.
Explain the role of each stage (water made settlement possible, pilgrimage helped the city grow).
Discover what “had not been discovered yet” tells us about order, and use so / because, after + noun or clause, where, to + verb and help + object + base verb.
Explain how another place changed over time.
content.pedagogy: Use a living timeline: Six volunteers hold event cards at the front and the class orders them after listening, justifying each place with a sentence from the text. The key discovery is the past perfect: Ask “When Abraham arrived, was Zamzam water there? Was it found later?” Learners find that “had not been discovered yet” means “not at that moment, but later”, and the next paragraph proves it (“After the discovery of Zamzam water …”).
priorKnowledge: Past simple; after, later, when; so and because.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Zamzam water was not known when Abraham (pbuh) arrived; “had not been discovered yet” means it was found later.
Zamzam and the Ka’ba have different roles: The water made settlement possible, and pilgrimage to the Ka’ba helped the city grow.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: past perfect passive had not been discovered yet (what had or had not happened before a past moment) · so for a result vs because for a reason · after + noun (after the discovery) vs after + clause (after Zamzam water was discovered) · where-clause for a place · to + verb for purpose · help + object + base verb.
Notice (Activity 1): “When Prophet Abraham (pbuh) brought his son Ishmael (pbuh) and his wife Hagar to the city, Zamzam water had not been discovered yet.” Ask: “At the moment they arrived, had anyone found the water? Which word tells you it happened later?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Turn the so-sentence into a because-sentence and “After the discovery of Zamzam water” into a clause, then choose where / to build / grow.
Likely errors: *had not discovered yet (active) · *Because Arabs accepted …, so the Ka’ba … (two linkers) · *a valley which no crops grow · *came for build · *helped the city growing.
Use (Activity 4): six connected sentences about another place that changed over time, with one “had not … yet” and one “helped … + base verb”.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Keep the time clause together, then pause: “When Prophet ABraham | brought his SON and his WIFE to the CIty, | ZAMzam WAter had NOT been disCOVered YET.” Stress NOT and YET.
Weak form: “had not been” — “been” is /bɪn/.
-ed endings: settled /d/, learned /d/, accepted /ɪd/, helped /t/.
Word focus: VAL-ley, pop-u-LA-tion, dis-COV-er-y, re-con-STRUCT, PIL-grim-age, RAP-id-ly.
beforeReading: Show five blank cards: water / people settle / a building / visitors / growth. Pairs predict the order in which a city in a dry valley could begin.
duringReading: Number the events on the timeline while listening.
Under each event write its job: Why did it matter?
Underline “had not been discovered yet” and find the sentence that shows when the water was found.
Circle so and the sentence that shows the result of pilgrimage.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the timeline visible.
Language Focus: Discover what the past perfect tells us (Activity 1), change result/reason and noun/clause (Activity 2), then choose where / to + verb / help + base verb (Activity 3).
Write six connected sentences about another place that changed over time (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Prediction: Pairs order five blank cards (water, people settle, building, visitors, growth) for a city in a dry valley; 5–12 Listen and read; 12–19 Living timeline: Six volunteers hold event cards at the front, the class orders them and gives one quoted sentence for each place in the line; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (When they arrived, had anyone found the water?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 31–38 Use: Learners write six sentences about how their town, a neighbourhood or their school changed (There was no … / had not … yet / after … / helped … grow), one pair reads and the class rebuilds the order; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did the discovery of Zamzam water make possible?
Why did the Ka’ba become a pilgrimage site, according to the chapter?
Which two events should not be merged into one?
interactiveTips: Use the Zamzam hotspot after learners have placed the discovery on the timeline.
Use the Abraham and Ishmael hotspot to show how the Ka’ba was built again.
Pause the audio after “had not been discovered yet” and ask: Before or after they arrived?

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give six event cards and the frames “When ____ arrived, ____ had not been ____ yet.” and “____, so ____. This helped ____ grow.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a six-sentence history of a place with a past perfect, after + noun and after + clause, a purpose phrase and a result with so.

formativeAssessment: Orders the stages accurately.
Explains the past perfect as “not yet at that past moment”.
Uses so / because, where, to + verb and help + base verb correctly.
expectedResponses: When Abraham (pbuh) brought Ishmael (pbuh) and Hagar, Zamzam water had not been discovered yet and there was no population; after its discovery the Jurhumites settled, later Abraham and Ishmael built the Ka’ba again, Arabs accepted their religion, so the Ka’ba became a pilgrimage site and this helped the city grow rapidly.
content.transferTask: Explain how one resource (water, a road, a school) helped a place you know grow.
content.teacherReflection: Did the living timeline keep sequence and cause apart, and did learners explain the past perfect by its meaning rather than its form?

classroomManagement.instructions: Six volunteers hold event cards at the front. The class puts them in order and gives one quoted sentence for each place in the line.
checkQuestions: How many volunteers? (six)
What does the class give for each card? (a quoted sentence)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that water comes before settlement. In Activity 1, ask whether anyone had found the water. After one pair reads, ask the class to rebuild the order.

exitTicket: Write one “had not … yet” sentence and one “helped … + base verb” sentence about your town.

rubricLevels.notYet: Give the first and last cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the role of each stage in the growth of the city.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What did this stage make possible?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the past perfect as “not yet at that moment”.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Had it happened when they arrived?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses so, because, to + verb and help + base verb.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one model of each.

interculturalFocus.notice: Mecca begins with Abraham, Hagar, Ishmael, Zamzam and the Jurhumites. A city's founding story is important in many cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: What is the founding story of Konya (the legend of the dervish who was told 'Kon ya!') or İstanbul (Byzas)? What is the founding story of Rome (Romulus and Remus)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Founding legends and historical facts are different. Learners say which is a legend and which is history.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note how city life began in Mecca.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners explain the beginning of Mecca in four steps.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner explains to a partner why the city grew rapidly. The partner restates it with “so”.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads paragraph 2. Listener notes what Ishmael (pbuh) learned. Writer writes it.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A classmate asks, “How did your town or city begin?” The learner answers and compares it with Mecca.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “City life began there with the building of the Ka’ba.” into their home language. How did each pair render “City life”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how the city of Mecca began. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The writer moves from an empty valley to a growing city. What links the steps?” (Water, people and the Ka’ba.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: The steps are in the right order. Learners name the Jurhumites.

objectives: Follow the stages of control over Mecca: Abraham (pbuh) returns to Palestine → the Khuza’a defeat the Jurhum → idol worship under Khuza’a rule → the Quraysh take over in the 5th century.
Separate three lanes of evidence (control, religion, economy) and explain why the dry land pushed Mecca towards trade.
Notice how after / later / under … rule guide the reader, and use started + -ing, took over and because … could not / so.
Explain a historical change in another place.
content.pedagogy: Draw three lanes on the board (Control / Religion / Economy). Pairs place every sentence in one lane, which stops learners from inventing links the text does not make (idol worship did not cause trade). Grammar is discovered through the sequencing task: Learners cannot order the sentences without reading the time words, so they find out what after, later and under … rule do before you name them.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 3 timeline; irregular past forms (came, took, forgot, made); because.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Trade is linked to the dry land and the impossibility of farming, not to idol worship.
The Khuza’a took control first; the Quraysh took over later, in the 5th century.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: time markers for stages (After …, Later, Later, in the 5th century, Under Khuza’a rule) · started + -ing for the beginning of a practice · took over = took control of · because … could not + verb for a limitation, and so for the result when the order changes.
Notice (Activity 1): learners put four parts of the chapter in time order, then say which words decided the order. Ask: “Why can ‘Under Khuza’a rule’ not come before the Khuza’a arrive?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose worshipping / over, then move the because-clause to the end and turn “because they produced many different goods” into a so-result.
Likely errors: *started worship · *took over of the city · *Because people could not farm …, so they made money … · a missing comma after a fronted because-clause.
Use (Activity 4): six connected sentences about a change in another historical place with one “under … rule” and one “because … could not …”.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Pause after each time frame: “LAter, | in the FIFTH CENtury, | the Quraysh tribe took OVer the CIty and the Ka’ba.”
In the phrasal verb the stress falls on the particle: “took OVER”.
-ed endings: completed /ɪd/, invited /ɪd/, returned /d/, defeated /ɪd/, worshipped /t/, traded /ɪd/, produced /t/.
Word focus: MIS-sion, de-FEAT-ed, WOR-ship-ping, bi-ZAN-tine (also BIZ-an-teen), EM-pires, in-do-NE-sia.
beforeReading: Draw three lanes (Control / Religion / Economy). Ask: “Mecca had no farms. How could people there make a living?” Keep ideas in the Economy lane as predictions.
duringReading: Mark each change of control with its time word.
Place idol worship in the Religion lane and the dry land → trade link in the Economy lane.
Underline “because … could not” and say what people did instead.
Note the empires and countries that were important for trade.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Order the stages of control (Activity 1), choose started worshipping / took over (Activity 2), then move and change the reason (Activity 3).
Write six connected sentences about a historical change in another place (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Three lanes on the board and the hook question (no farms — how do people live?); 4–11 Listen and read; 11–19 Lane sort in pairs: Every sentence goes into Control, Religion or Economy with its time word or linking word underlined, then a whole-class check (Does any arrow go from Religion to Economy? The text does not say so); 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs with the question “Which words decided the order?”, Activities 2–3 individually with pair checking; 31–38 Use: Six sentences about how control or life changed in a place learners know from history lessons (after, later, under … rule, started + -ing, because … could not), partners circle every time marker; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Who controlled Mecca at each stage?
What changed in religion under Khuza’a rule?
Why did people in Mecca make money through trade?
interactiveTips: Use the Khuza’a Rule hotspot for the Control and Religion lanes and the Trade Economy hotspot for the Economy lane.
Replay the dry-land sentence before accepting any cause statement.
Ask learners to label every link “happened after” or “happened because”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the lanes with one sentence already placed in each and the frames “Under ____ rule, people started ____-ing.” and “Because people could not ____, they ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six sentences about a change of rule in history with after, later, under … rule, took over, and one reason written in two ways (because / so).

objectives: Explain three conditions that made Mecca a busy trading city: Its location, the trade agreements of Hashim and the Quraysh leaders, and the sacred months.
Explain what people did in the sacred months and why more people could visit the city to perform Hajj.

Discover the difference between because + clause and because of + noun, and use allow + person + to, fixed phrases (focus on, stay away from), From + time, make + object + adjective and to + verb for purpose.
Explain how conditions can create an opportunity in another place.
content.pedagogy: Draw a “conditions → opportunity” diagram: Three boxes (location / agreements / sacred months) with arrows to “busy and wealthy city” and “more visitors for Hajj”. Every arrow must carry a word from the text (because, allowed … to, made … safer, because of). The grammar discovery starts from the first and last sentences of the chapter: Learners compare what follows because and because of and state the rule themselves.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 4: trade as the answer to the dry land; because; can / could.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The sacred months were not only about trade: People focused on worship, showed respect and stayed away from fighting.
Hashim did not act alone: “He and the Quraysh leaders made special trade agreements”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: because + subject + verb vs because of + noun phrase · allow + person + to + verb · fixed phrases focus on / show respect / stay away from · From + time with the past simple · make + object + comparative adjective (made the region safer) · to + verb for purpose.
Notice (Activity 1): Compare “Because Mecca was in the middle of important trade routes, …” and “Because of this safe atmosphere, …”. Ask: “Do both give a reason? What comes after each one?” Learners state the rule before they choose.
Build (Activities 2–3): Match the phrases with their meanings, then choose From / safer / to perform.
Likely errors: *because of Mecca was in the middle … · *allowed merchants travel · *stayed away of fighting · *Since the early 6th century, Mecca became … · *made the region more safer / to be safer.
Use (Activity 4): six connected sentences about how conditions created an opportunity somewhere else.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Two reason frames, two rhythms: “beCAUSE MECca was in the MIDdle of imPORtant TRADE routes, |” / “beCAUSE of this SAFE ATmosphere, |”.
Read the four months as a list with a short pause at each comma and a fall on the last name.
-ed endings: helped /t/, allowed /d/, focused /t/, showed /d/, stayed /d/.
Word focus: WEALTH-y (/θ/), a-GREE-ments, e-CON-o-my, AT-mos-phere, MER-chants, e-thi-O-pi-a.

Replay the first and last sentences back-to-back so learners hear because and because of.
Keep worship and trade on separate labels in the diagram.

objectives: Explain how pilgrimage practices that continued before Islam kept Mecca active and helped business grow.
Name the three fairs and put “attended the fairs → went to Arafat” in order.
Explain how lending money with usury made the rich richer and the poor poorer.
Discover what “continued to” shows and use keep + object + adjective, help + object + base verb, first … and then … and make + object + comparative.
content.pedagogy: Use a flow chart that splits at the end: Practices at the Ka’ba → an active city → fairs → business grows → Quraysh control the main trade routes and wealth → usury → two arrows (rich richer / poor poorer). Learners fill every box with a quoted phrase. The discovery starts with the first sentence: “Was visiting the Ka’ba new?” Learners use Chapter 3 (“the Ka’ba became a pilgrimage site”) to prove it was not, and so they find the meaning of “continued to” themselves.
priorKnowledge: Chapters 3 and 5: pilgrimage and trade; comparatives (richer, poorer).
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Continued to” does not mean that the visits started at this time.
The chapter does not call trade itself unfair; it names lending money with usury as the practice that made the rich richer and the poor poorer.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: continue to + verb for an action that did not stop · keep + object + adjective (kept Mecca active) · help + object + base verb (helped business grow) · first … and then … with two past verbs · make + object + comparative adjective, without repeating the verb after and (made the rich richer and the poor poorer).
Notice (Activity 1): “Before Islam, idol worshippers continued to visit and walk around the Ka’ba.” Ask: “Was this a new practice? What did Chapter 3 tell us?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Find and fix kept … to be active / helped … growing / then go, then rebuild the last sentence of the chapter.
Likely errors: *kept Mecca to be active · *helped business growing · *attended … first and then go · *made the rich more rich.
Use (Activity 4): six connected sentences about a system and its different effects on two groups.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrastive stress in the last sentence: “This made the RICH RICHer | and the POOR POORer.”
Sequence: “People atTENDed these FAIRS FIRST | and THEN went to ARafat.”
-ed endings: continued /d/, attended /ɪd/, controlled /d/, used /d/.
Word focus: WOR-ship-pers, U-su-ry (/ˈjuːʒəri/), WIDE-spread, AC-tive, SEA-son, PIL-grim-age.

duringReading: Box the practices that kept Mecca active.

Mark who controlled the trade routes and wealth.
Draw two arrows from usury: The rich / the poor.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.

content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: A festival in town — who earns money, and does everyone earn the same?; 4–11 Listen and read; 11–19 Split flow chart in pairs: practices → active city → fairs → business → Quraysh control → usury → two arrows, every box with a quoted phrase; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery with Chapter 3 as evidence (Was visiting the Ka’ba new?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners say one more “made … -er” sentence; 31–38 Use: Six sentences about a system with two different effects (for example a price rise in the school canteen or a new shopping center), partners check that each group has its own result; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What kept Mecca active during the pilgrimage season?
In what order did people attend the fairs and go to Arafat?
Why did usury make the gap between the rich and the poor bigger?
interactiveTips: Use the Trade Fairs hotspot for the fairs and the Usury hotspot for the split at the end of the flow chart.
Replay the last sentence: Learners point left at “rich” and right at “poor”.
Keep the focus on usury; do not equate business activity itself with unfairness.

objectives: Explain how usury, high interest, drinking and gambling pushed many people into debt and widened the gap between social classes.
Contrast the lives of the rich and the poor with quoted evidence.
Recognize that the leaders’ question “why Muhammad should be the leader” is an objection that shows their values, not the writer’s view.
Use while for contrast, “nothing was more important than”, could not + verb, because of + noun and push … into.
content.pedagogy: Build a two-column contrast (the rich / the poor and weak): gold plates and silver cups on one side, debt, struggling to survive, orphans and property taken by force on the other. Then turn to viewpoint: Ask “Whose opinion is ‘while they were rich and important’?” Learners discover that a reported question can show a group’s values without the writer agreeing. The word-bank activity becomes a cause map: could not → because of → pushed … deeper into.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 6 usury; while from Chapter 1; reported speech with asked.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The writer does not agree that wealth should decide leadership; he reports the leaders’ objection.
“Powerful people were usually merchants who lent money with usury” does not mean that all merchants were cruel.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: reported question as an objection (asked why Muhammad should be the leader while they were rich and important) · while for contrast, first or second in the sentence · the most important = nothing was more important than … · could not + verb for inability · because of + noun phrase · push + person + deeper into + noun.
Notice (Activity 1): Read the reported question and ask: “Did the leaders really want information? Which words show what they thought gives a person the right to lead?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Move the while-clause and say the superlative with “nothing was more important than”, then complete could not / because of / into.
Likely errors: *because high interest · *could not paid back · *pushed people deeper in debt · *While the rich lived in luxury, but the poor ….
Use (Activity 4): six connected sentences about inequality in another school, workplace or community situation, including one reported objection.
content.pronunciationFocus:
A contrast needs two clear parts: “While the RICH lived in LUXury | with GOLD PLATES and SILver CUPS, | the POOR STRUGgled to surVIVE.”
Reported question, falling tune (it is not a real question): “some rich LEADers asked WHY MuHAMmad should be the LEADer↘”.
Silent b: debt /det/, debts /dets/.
Word focus: LUX-u-ry (/ˈlʌkʃəri/), OR-phans, PROP-er-ty, GAM-bling, IN-ter-est, sur-VIVE.
beforeReading: Write two phrases on the board: “gold plates” / “no food for tomorrow”. Ask what could cause such a gap in one city. Keep the answers as predictions.
duringReading: Two columns: The rich / the poor and weak, each item with a quoted phrase.
Mark three things that kept people in debt.
Underline the leaders’ reported question and label it “their view”.
Circle the sentence about orphans and property.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Decide what the reported question shows (Activity 1), move the while-contrast and rephrase the superlative (Activity 2), then complete could not / because of / into (Activity 3).
Write six connected sentences about inequality in another situation, including one reported objection (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “gold plates” / “no food for tomorrow” on the board, pairs predict what could cause the gap; 4–11 Listen and read; 11–18 Two-column contrast plus a cause map for debt (usury → high interest → could not pay back → drinking and gambling pushed people deeper into debt), each link with a quoted phrase; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Whose opinion is this?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 31–38 Use: Six sentences about an unfair situation at school or work (for example only some students can pay for a school trip) with while, because of, could not and one “asked why …” objection, a volunteer reads and the class names the viewpoint; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What kept many people in debt, according to the chapter?

interactiveTips: Use the Class Gap hotspot for the two-column contrast and the Weak People hotspot for orphans and property.
Replay the reported question and ask learners to name the words that show the leaders’ view.
Do not role-play the leaders’ objection; analyse it as a viewpoint.

objectives: Explain why tribes were the center of Arab society: In a hard desert life, the tribe protected life and property.
Explain, with the chapter’s reasons, why physical strength, sons and ancestors were valued.
Discover the meaning of had to, in every situation and even when, and use so / because / to + verb and without → if.
Discuss loyalty to a group together with its limits.
content.pedagogy: Use a “protection and pressure” balance: On one side what the tribe gave (safety of life and property), on the other what it demanded (work for the tribe, follow it, protect and honor it even when it did something wrong). Learners then meet the language of duty: Matching had to, in every situation and even when with their meanings shows them how strong tribal loyalty was. The word-bank activity turns the first paragraphs into a result–reason–purpose chain.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 1: tribes as the basis of society; so and because; if-sentences with could.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The chapter does not present tribes only negatively: They gave protection.
“Even when the tribe did something wrong” describes the rule of the time; the chapter does not present it as a good rule.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: had to for a past duty · in every situation / even when for the strength of the duty · so (result) because (reason), To + verb (purpose) · without + noun = if … did not have … · could not easily for limited ability.
Notice (Activity 1): learners match five phrases with their meanings, then answer: “Which words show that the duty did not stop even in a bad case?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete the lines with so / because / To, then rewrite “Without a tribe, people could not easily protect their lives or property.” with if.
Likely errors: *For earn respect · *because of they were fighters · *If people did not have a tribe, they cannot … · *even the tribe did something wrong (when missing).
Use (Activity 4): six connected sentences about rules, support and consequences in a group, team or club, with one “had to … even when …”.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Result and purpose frames: “Life in the DEsert was VEry HARD, | so PHYsical STRENGTH was exTREMEly imPORtant.” / “To earn reSPECT from other TRIBES, | …”.
Stress the limit of the duty: “in EVery situAtion, | EVen when the TRIBE did something WRONG.”
Weak form: “had to” /ˈhæd tə/.
Word focus: AN-ces-tors, PHYS-i-cal, pro-TEC-tion, VAL-u-a-ble, LOY-al-ty, HON-or (silent h).
beforeReading: Ask: “What does a team give you, and what does it ask from you?” Two columns on the board: gives / asks.
duringReading: Mark the reason physical strength was important.
Mark why families wanted many sons.
Underline what happened to a person outside tribal protection.
Box the most important rule and the words “even when”.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.

content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: What does a team give you and what does it ask from you? two columns on the board; 4–11 Listen and read; 11–18 Protection and pressure balance in pairs: Gives (safety of life and property) / demands (work for the tribe, follow it, protect and honor it even when it was wrong), each item with a quoted phrase; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs, then the whole-class question “Which words show the duty never stopped?”, Activities 2–3 in pairs; 31–38 Use: Six sentences about a team, club or class with had to, without … / if … and one “even when” sentence, followed by a one-minute pair discussion: Should loyalty continue when the group is wrong?; 38–40 Exit ticket.

Why were strength, sons and ancestors valued, according to the chapter?
What does “even when the tribe did something wrong” show about tribal loyalty?

What does each item need? (a quoted phrase)

objectives: Explain how women’s lives differed depending on wealth and family, with Khadija as the chapter’s example of a rich woman.
Describe slavery in old Mecca factually and explain why owning many slaves was a sign of wealth, without dramatising it.
Explain three jobs of poetry and why poets were “like the media of the people”.
Discover what “depending on” shows and why the chapter uses the passive for slaves, and correct could + base verb, because vs because of and parallel verbs.
content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 builds meaning in three calm stations (women / slavery / poetry), each with a guiding question and evidence cards written by learners. The teacher rereads the slavery paragraph once in an even voice; it is discussed as a system and never acted out. Lesson 2 opens the language: Learners discover that “depending on” introduces the factor that makes lives different, that “were bought and sold” keeps the slaves in focus, and that a list of actions keeps the same verb form.
priorKnowledge: however; the passive was/were + past participle; the idea of rights.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The chapter does not say that all women had no rights: Rich women like Khadija could run their own businesses.
Poets are compared with the media because they kept history alive, praised tribes and criticized enemies; they were not journalists.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: depending on + noun for a factor that changes something · However to turn to the other side · passive were bought and sold to keep the affected people in focus · an -ing form as subject (owning many slaves was a sign of wealth) · could + base verb · because + clause vs because of + noun · parallel past verbs in a list (kept …, praised …, and criticized …) · like + noun for comparison (like the media).
Notice (Activity 1): “Before Islam, the life of Arab women was very different depending on their wealth and family.” Ask: “What made one woman’s life different from another’s? Which words tell you?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Rewrite the passive sentence in the active and the -ing subject as an if-clause, then find and fix could ran / because of they / criticizing.
Likely errors: *depending of · *could ran · *because of they wanted · *kept …, praised …, and criticizing ….
Use (Activity 4): six connected sentences about unequal roles and social functions in another community.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Keep the factor together: “was VEry DIFFerent | dePENDing on their WEALTH and FAMily.”
Passive with weak “were”: “were BOUGHT and SOLD” (/wə/).
Parallel list, rise – rise – fall: “kept tribal HIStory aLIVE↗, | PRAISED TRIBES↗, | and CRITicized ENemies↘.”
-ed endings: faced /t/, praised /d/, criticized /d/.
Word focus: SLA-ver-y, BRU-tal, TREAT-ment, e-CON-o-my, ME-di-a, BUSI-ness-es (/ˈbɪznəsɪz/).
beforeReading: Lesson 1: ask: “Can two people in the same city have very different chances in life? What could make the difference?” Collect factors (money, family, place) as predictions.
duringReading: Station A (women): What could rich women do, and what did many poor women face?
Station B (slavery): How were slaves treated, and what was owning many slaves a sign of?
Station C (poetry): List the three jobs of poetry.
Underline “depending on” and “However”.
afterReading: Lesson 1: Quick Challenge plus a bridge note with one fact from each station.
Lesson 2: Language Focus: Discover “depending on” (Activity 1), rewrite the passive and the -ing subject (Activity 2), then fix could / because / the parallel list (Activity 3).
Write six connected sentences about unequal roles and social functions in another community (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Hook: Same city, different chances — what makes the difference? factors on the board; 5–13 Listen and read, then the teacher rereads the slavery paragraph once in a calm, even voice; 13–27 Three stations in groups (women / slavery / poetry): each group writes two evidence cards with a quoted phrase, then rotates once to check another group’s cards; 27–33 Whole-class check: Poets were “like the media” — what did they do?; 33–37 Quick Challenge; 37–40 Bridge note: One fact from each station; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the three stations from memory; 4–12 Language Focus Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (What made the difference?), then learners say one “depending on” sentence about school life; 12–22 Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners explain why the chapter keeps the slaves as the subject; 22–33 Use: Six sentences about roles in another community (depending on, however, because, one passive, one parallel list of three verbs); 33–38 Pairs check every list for parallel verbs and every because / because of; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How did wealth and family change a woman’s life, according to the chapter?
Why does the chapter say that slaves “were bought and sold” instead of naming who bought and sold them?
In what ways were poets “like the media of the people”?
interactiveTips: Use the Status of Women hotspot at Station A and the Poets as Media hotspot at Station C.
Replay the passive sentence only for language analysis, never for dramatic effect.
Do not role-play enslavement or mistreatment.

content.teacherReflection: Did learners handle slavery calmly and as a system, and did they discover why the passive keeps the affected people in focus?

objectives: Describe religious life before Islam with accurate quantities: Most people worshipped idols, only a few followed religions like Christianity, and some people (the Hanifs) followed the old religion of Abraham (pbuh).
Explain the belief reported in the chapter: people believed in Allah as the Creator but also worshipped idols because they thought the idols helped them talk to Allah.
Separate the writer’s own statements from reported beliefs (thought, believed).
Use most / only a few / including, the passive were kept and before + -ing.
content.pedagogy: Start with a quantity line on the board (all — most — some — only a few — none) and let learners place each group from the chapter on it. Then sort sentences into “the writer says it” / “people thought or believed it”. This is the discovery: Learners notice that thought and believed report a belief without the writer accepting it. The drag-and-drop activity then confirms what they have already found.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 3: the religion of Abraham (pbuh); the quantity words most, some, few.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Most” does not mean “all”; the chapter also names the Hanifs and people who followed religions like Christianity.
“They thought these idols helped them talk to Allah” reports their belief; the text does not present it as true.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: reporting a belief with thought / believed (in) vs the writer’s own statement · quantity words most / only a few / some · including for examples from a larger group · passive were kept for location · before + -ing = before + subject + verb.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort six parts of the chapter into “the writer says it directly” and “the writer reports what people thought or believed”. Ask: “Does the writer agree that the idols helped people talk to Allah? How do you know?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose most / Only a few / including, then rewrite “They were kept …” in the active and “before making decisions” with a full clause.
Likely errors: *all people in Arabia worshipped idols (overclaim) · *only a little people · *360 idols, included Lat … · *before make decisions.
Use (Activity 4): six connected sentences about the beliefs or habits of a group without overgeneralizing.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Quantity words carry the stress: “MOST people in Arabia worshipped IDols. ONly a FEW people followed …”.
Reported belief: “They THOUGHT | these idols helped them TALK to alLAH.”
Number: “three hundred and sixty idols”.
Word focus: I-dols, chris-ti-AN-i-ty, su-per-STI-tions, O-mens, SOOTH-say-ers, cre-A-tor.
beforeReading: Draw a quantity line: All — most — some — only a few — none. Ask: “Which word fits the students in our class who like football?” Practise precise quantity before reading.
duringReading: Place each group on the quantity line (idol worshippers, followers of religions like Christianity, Hanifs).
Underline every thought / believed.
Mark the sentence that names the most important religious activity.
Circle “before making decisions”.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Sort fact and reported belief (Activity 1), choose the accurate quantity words (Activity 2), then rewrite the passive and before + -ing (Activity 3).
Write six connected sentences about a group’s beliefs or habits without overgeneralizing (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Quantity line on the board, quick practice with class examples; 4–11 Listen and read; 11–18 Pairs place the groups from the chapter on the quantity line and underline every thought / believed; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Does the writer agree? How do you know?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 31–38 Use: Six sentences about habits or beliefs in another community or in your class (most, some, only a few, people think that …, before + -ing), partners underline any “all” or “everyone” and check it; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which words does the chapter use to show how many people worshipped idols?
What did people believe about Allah, and what did they also do?
How can we tell the writer’s statements from reported beliefs?
interactiveTips: Use the 360 Idols hotspot for the majority pattern and the Hanifs hotspot for the exception.
Replay “They thought these idols helped them talk to Allah.” and ask whose idea it is.
Keep the lesson descriptive; do not go beyond the idols the chapter names.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the quantity line with the three groups as cards and the frames “Most people ____. Only a few ____.” and “They thought that ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six sentences about a community with three different quantity words, one reported belief, one passive and one before + -ing.

formativeAssessment: Uses quantity words that match the evidence.
Separates reported belief from the writer’s statement.
Uses including, the passive and before + -ing correctly.
expectedResponses: Most people in Arabia and in Mecca worshipped idols, only a few followed religions like Christianity, and the Hanifs followed the old religion of Abraham (pbuh); people believed in Allah as the Creator but also worshipped idols because they thought the idols helped them talk to Allah.
content.transferTask: Describe a habit in your class or town accurately with most / some / only a few, and add one belief people have about it with “People think that …”.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep reported beliefs separate from the writer’s statements and choose quantity words that match the evidence?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, place the groups from the chapter on the quantity line: most, some, only a few. Underline every “thought” and “believed”.
checkQuestions: What words are on the quantity line? (most, some, only a few)
What do you underline? (thought and believed)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that “only a few” followed other religions. In Activity 1, ask whether the writer agrees. In the Use task, ask partners to check every all or everyone.

interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How do English texts describe the beliefs of a group respectfully ('they believed that', 'in their tradition')? Which Turkish phrases do the same ('inanışlarına göre')?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners use 'most', 'some' and 'only a few' carefully, as the chapter does, to avoid stereotypes.

noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners explain in two sentences why people worshipped idols though they believed in Allah.

mediationTasks.pairRoles: Questioner asks “What did people check before making decisions?”. Finder reads the answer. Summarizer paraphrases it.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “Are there superstitions in your culture?” The learner gives one and explains why it is not true.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Pilgrimage to the Ka’ba was the most important religious activity in early Arabia.” into their home language. Which word did each pair choose for “pilgrimage”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what people believed in old Mecca. Next lesson ask what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The writer says ‘actually believed in one main God’. Why does the word ‘actually’ matter?” (It corrects what the reader may think.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners keep the idols, the Hanifs and the superstitions apart. They name three idols.

objectives: Explain the chapter’s general idea (politics, economics and religion are connected) and how it leads to the dislike of Islam by powerful groups in Mecca.
Contrast two reactions to the Qur’an: People who became Muslims and many leaders who ignored it.
Discover what “That is why” connects and use was/were going to, hear + person + base verb, make + person + base verb, However and for + a period of time.
Explain a social change and two reactions to it in another context.
content.pedagogy: Start with the logic chain at the top of the chapter: Two general statements in the present simple → “That is why” → a result in the past. Learners draw it as three boxes and discover that “That” points back to the ideas before it. Then pairs build a reaction chart (accepted / resisted) with evidence. The word-bank activity shows why “However”, not “So”, introduces the leaders’ reaction.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 10 religious life; the present simple for general truths; however.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “That is why” does not explain why politics and religion are connected; it introduces a result of that connection.
The chapter does not say that everyone rejected the message: Some people became Muslims and were sure it was from Allah.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: That is why + result · present simple for general truths vs past simple for history · was/were going to + verb for a future seen from the past · hear + person + base verb (heard Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) read the Qur’an) · make + person + base verb (made them feel great respect) · However for an opposite reaction · for + a period of time.
Notice (Activity 1): Read the first three sentences and ask: “Does ‘That is why’ give a reason or a result? What does ‘That’ point back to?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose were going to be / read, then complete feel / However / for.
Likely errors: *They are going to be different (the past viewpoint lost) · *heard him to read · *made them to feel · *So, many leaders ignored … · *since 13 years.
Use (Activity 4): six connected sentences about a social change and two different reactions to it.
content.pronunciationFocus:
General statements: short, even and falling: “POLitics, | ecoNOMics, | and reLIgion are conNECTed↘.”
Pause before the result: “THAT is WHY | POWerful groups in MECca | did NOT like ISlam.”
Weak forms: “were going to be” (/wə/), “for 13 years” (/fə/).
Numbers: “about five thousand to ten thousand people”.
Word focus: POL-i-tics, e-co-NOM-ics, com-MU-ni-ty, ig-NORED, re-SPECT, DEEP-ly.
beforeReading: Ask: “Can a new idea change who has power and money? Give one example from today, for example a new app or a new rule.” Keep answers short.
duringReading: Draw the logic chain from the first three sentences.
Two columns: accepted / resisted, each with a quoted phrase.
Underline “were going to be” and “heard … read”.
Note how long the Prophet (pbuh) taught in Mecca and how many people lived there.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Discover what “That is why” connects (Activity 1), choose were going to be / read (Activity 2), then complete feel / However / for (Activity 3).
Write six connected sentences about a social change and two reactions (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: Can a new idea change who has power and money? one modern example per pair; 4–11 Listen and read; 11–18 Logic chain on the board (two general statements → That is why → result), then pairs build the reaction chart accepted / resisted with evidence; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (reason or result?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners explain why “So” is wrong in Activity 3; 31–38 Use: Six sentences about a change at school or in the community (a new rule, a new club) with That is why, was/were going to, when … and however, two volunteers read; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did powerful groups in Mecca dislike Islam, according to the first paragraph?
How did the Qur’an affect those who became Muslims?
Why does the chapter use “However” for the leaders’ reaction?
interactiveTips: Use the A New Community hotspot for the first paragraph and The Qur’an hotspot for the two reactions.
Replay “When they heard Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) read the Qur’an …” and ask what they heard and how they felt.
Do not infer motives beyond what the chapter states.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the logic-chain boxes and the frames “____. That is why ____.”, “When they heard ____, they ____.” and “However, ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six sentences with a general statement, That is why, was/were going to, hear / make + person + base verb and a contrasting reaction with however.

formativeAssessment: Explains the logic chain.
Contrasts the two reactions with evidence.
Uses That is why, was/were going to and the base verb after hear / make correctly.
expectedResponses: Beliefs shape how people live, so a new belief could change power and wealth, and that is why powerful groups in Mecca did not like Islam; some people who heard the Qur’an were sure it was from Allah and were deeply changed, but many leaders ignored it; the Prophet (pbuh) taught in Mecca for 13 years.

content.teacherReflection: Did learners see “That is why” as pointing back to general ideas, and did they keep the two reactions distinct?

What do you add? (evidence)

objectives: Explain why the leaders of Quraysh did not accept Islam: Their power, the respect of other tribes, their prestige as caretakers of pilgrimage and their unity.
Explain the changes Islam brought (the Qur’an forbade usury and allowed only honest trade, and Islam commanded zakat and sadaqah to help the poor) and why they challenged the leaders.
Discover how “almost none” limits a claim and how “felt that” reports the leaders’ view.

content.pedagogy: Build a “what they wanted to keep / what Islam changed” chart and require a quoted phrase for every item. content.grammarFocus:

objectives: Trace how opposition grew: mocking → violent opposition after the Qur’an criticized the idols → a social and economic boycott (617–620).

content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 builds an escalation staircase with three steps (mocking / violent opposition / boycott), each with a quoted phrase and the event that caused the change. The teacher reads Bilal’s paragraph once, calmly; it is discussed only as evidence of how unprotected people suffered and is never acted out. Lesson 2 is about language: The sequencing activity lets learners discover how At first … only, But when and went further mark each step before you name them, and the error correction fixes the repeated past, the reported order and the purpose phrase.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 8: protection came from tribes; Chapter 9: slavery; the past simple.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The opposition was not violent from the beginning: “At first, the leaders of Mecca only mocked Islam.”

content.grammarFocus:
Targets: escalation markers (At first … only, But when …, went further) · whenever + past simple, past simple for a reaction that happened every time · order + person + to + verb · to + verb for purpose · those without + noun to describe a group · often + past simple for a habit.
Notice (Activity 1): learners put four sentences in order and answer: “Which words show that each step is more serious than the one before?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Find and fix laugh / ordered him give up / for support, then decide who “those without powerful friends” are.
Likely errors: *Whenever … walked by, they laugh … · *ordered him give up · *for support the Muslims · “those without powerful friends” read as “people with no friends”.
Use (Activity 4): six connected sentences about a situation that became more serious and someone who acted to help.
content.pronunciationFocus:

-ed endings: mocked /t/, laughed /t/, criticized /d/, warned /d/, ordered /d/, helped /t/.
Dates: “between six seventeen and six twenty”.
Read Bilal’s paragraph slowly and evenly, without a dramatic voice.
Word focus: VI-o-lent, ab-ys-SIN-i-an, BOY-cott, ec-o-NOM-ic, be-LIEV-ers, op-po-SI-tion.
beforeReading: Lesson 1: draw an empty three-step staircase. Ask: “How can a conflict become more serious step by step?” Learners suggest neutral steps (words, actions, rules).
duringReading: Write one step on each stair (mocking / violent opposition / boycott) with the event that caused the change.

objectives: Describe the human impact of the boycott calmly and factually (no food, hunger, tree leaves, the cries of hungry children).

Explain the leaders’ reasons for hostility: pride in old beliefs, idols that brought money, trade and power, the fear of losing wealth and influence, not wanting to accept judgement after death, and the fear of losing tribal protection.
Discover why the chapter says “could be heard” without naming a listener, and turn so-results into because-reasons and back.
Use stop + -ing, want + to + verb and parallel -ing forms after a preposition.
content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 separates two questions: “What happened to people?” (paragraph 1, reread calmly by the teacher) and “Why did the leaders resist?” (paragraphs 2–3). Learners build a reason web with at least four reasons from the text. Lesson 2 turns to language: The passive “could be heard everywhere” shows how widespread the hunger was without naming a listener, and the so ↔ because transformation shows that cause and effect stay the same when the linker changes.
priorKnowledge: Chapters 12–13: the leaders’ interests and the boycott; so and because; -ing after prepositions.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The leaders’ hostility is not explained by one reason only; the chapter gives several.
“Could be heard everywhere” does not mean that nobody heard the cries; the listener simply does not matter.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: passive with could (could be heard) to keep the focus on the cries · so for a result ↔ because for a reason · -ing after meant / feared (meant losing, feared losing) · stop + -ing vs stop to + verb · want + to + verb · a parallel -ing list after for (hurting …, making …, drinking …, or doing …).
Notice (Activity 1): “The cries of hungry children could be heard everywhere.” Ask: “Who heard the cries? Why does the writer not tell us?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Turn the so-sentence into a because-sentence and the because-sentence into a so-sentence, then fix stop worship / did not want changing / drink.

The -ing list rises on each item and falls on the last one.
Word focus: sur-VIVE, HOS-tile, PUN-ish-ment, IN-flu-ence, AL-co-hol, LOY-al-ty.

objectives: Explain how strong tribal loyalty made freedom of choice difficult and why leaving the tribe’s way was “almost like being stateless today”.

content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 sorts the chapter into three strands: Pressure (tribal loyalty, losing protection, preventing people from becoming Muslim), claim (what the leaders said) and the writer’s view (a better unity, every person is important). Learners put a speaker label on every sentence. priorKnowledge: Chapter 8 tribal loyalty; Chapter 1 Jahiliyyah; reported speech with said; could for possibility.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “The Quraysh leaders said Islam was breaking up families and destroying unity” is a reported claim, not the writer’s view.
“Almost like being stateless today” is a careful comparison with today, not a description of states in old Arabia.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: reported claim (The Quraysh leaders said …) vs the writer’s view (In reality, …) · so + adjective + that for degree and result · If …, … could … for a possible consequence · prevent + person + from + -ing · tell + person + to + verb · almost like + -ing for a careful comparison · based on for a foundation · make + person + comparative in the negative.

Likely errors: *such strong that · *prevent … to become · *told people be · “In reality” used to introduce the claim instead of the answer.
Use (Activity 4): five or six connected sentences about a social pressure and a fairer alternative.
content.pronunciationFocus:
