metadata.title: Mecca B1 — Teacher Guide
metadata.subtitle: TYMM-aligned guide with chapter-specific support, inductive grammar and 40-minute lesson plans
metadata.estimatedDuration: 15 chapter units: Chapters 1–8 and 10–12 are planned for 40 minutes; Chapters 9 and 13–15 are planned as 40 + 40 minutes. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetAudience: B1 English learners, especially upper-secondary students.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow connected historical and social texts, find evidence, keep quantities and viewpoints accurate, and produce short connected explanations with support.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B1 reading, listening, speaking and writing through the story of Mecca before Islam — its society, economy, tribal and religious life — and the early response to Islam, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively, as the Maarif Model expects for English: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does (the rule is confirmed only afterwards), then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world. Longer or more sensitive chapters are divided into two 40-minute lessons rather than compressed. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/yabanci-dil-alan-becerileri.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 15 Quick Challenges, text-evidence and viewpoint checks, chapter Language Focus tasks and production, exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Language Review, Vocabulary Challenge, the Master Glossary as a reference, and the Final Challenge.

formative: Language Focus: Noticing and controlled practice

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs, with a short chapter-specific prediction, question, card task or board diagram.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist, then read and follow the chapter’s own evidence structure: power map, definition, timeline, lanes, conditions, contrast, quantity line, viewpoint, escalation or reason web — keeping quantity words and reported views exactly as written.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B1 transfer about the learners’ own world. In 40 + 40 chapters, Lesson 1 secures meaning and evidence and Lesson 2 develops language and production.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Prioritise chapter Word Notes and the words needed for the chapter’s key relationship (cause, contrast, quantity, viewpoint).
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context, hotspot or audio before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus production, exit tickets, the Language Review and the Vocabulary Challenge.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us? Whose view is this?), let learners formulate the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practise it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer. Do not replace the chapter work with unrelated grammar drills.
grammarSequence: Ch1: For this reason; because vs because of; while-contrast; passive focus (were treated); describe … as
Ch2: explanation order (To understand …, we must first …; this city); describe … as; when-clause; inserted definition
Ch3: past perfect passive (had not been discovered yet); so vs because; after + noun / clause; where; to + verb; help + object + verb
Ch4: stage markers (after, later, under … rule); started + -ing; took over; because … could not / so
Ch5: because vs because of; allow … to; focus on / stay away from; From + time; make + object + adjective; to + verb
Ch6: continue to; keep + object + adjective; help + object + verb; first … then; made the rich richer
Ch7: reported question as objection; while; nothing more important than; could not; because of; push … into
Ch8: had to; in every situation / even when; so / because / to + verb; without → if
Ch9: depending on; however; passive focus; -ing subject; could + verb; because vs because of; parallel verbs
Ch10: reported belief (thought, believed); most / only a few / including; passive were kept; before + -ing
Ch11: That is why; was/were going to; hear / make + person + verb; however; for + period
Ch12: almost none; felt that → because; -ing subject = It was important to; forbade / commanded / turned against
Ch13: escalation markers; whenever + past; order … to; to + verb; those without …
Ch14: could be heard; so ↔ because; meant / feared + -ing; stop + -ing; want to; parallel -ing list
Ch15: reported claim vs In reality; so … that; If … could; prevent … from; tell … to; almost like; based on

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration for gist, sequence, cause, contrast, quantity and viewpoint.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify main ideas, direct evidence, cause-result chains, contrast, quantity limits, reported beliefs and claims.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: explain relationships, compare groups, report viewpoints, justify claims and discuss sensitive topics respectfully.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce connected B1 paragraphs using evidence, chapter patterns and short reflection about the learners’ own world.

valuesFocus: D5 Sensitivity — sensitivity to vulnerability, inequality, exploitation and collective harm
D6 Honesty — evidence-based definition, accurate reporting and avoidance of overgeneralization
D9 Compassion — non-harm and humane response under pressure
D14 Respect — dignity, non-discrimination and respectful disagreement
D16 Responsibility — responsible use of power, wealth and community roles
D20 Helpfulness — support for people facing exclusion or pressure
languageFocus: Every one of the 15 story chapters has an active Language Focus set built as notice → build → use.
Use Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence: Ask what the form does, or whose view it expresses, before naming it.
Let learners answer first; the explanation shown after each answer confirms the rule they have found.
At B1 the last step is always connected production about the learners’ own world, not a retelling of the chapter.
For 40 + 40 chapters, use the second lesson for Language Focus and connected production rather than re-reading the whole story.
After Chapter 15, follow the student sequence: Knowledge Check → Language Review → Vocabulary Challenge → Master Glossary → Final Challenge.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the reasoning target: One evidence sentence at a time, selected vocabulary, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by combining more chapter patterns or adding a second evidence relationship, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful discussion
notes: Keep religious and historical claims within the wording of the story.
Preserve quantity words and qualifiers such as “most”, “only a few”, “almost none”, “often” and “usually”.
Keep the beliefs and claims of historical groups (“they thought”, “the leaders said”) separate from the writer’s statements.
Discuss slavery, Bilal’s persecution, the boycott and hunger factually and calmly; never role-play violence, mockery or suffering.
Do not generalise about women, tribes, merchants or leaders beyond the chapter’s wording.
Qur’anic verses and references, prophetic sayings, prayers and poem lines are read, explained and matched to meanings; they are never gapped, “corrected” or rewritten.
Do not introduce legends, events, dates or biographical details that are not in this B1 book.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The story of Mecca before Islam raises questions every society faces: Who is protected, how wealth is shared, how people without power are treated, and how a community can be united by justice rather than by pressure.

themes.title: Protection for those without power:
themes.description: Poor and weak people lived in misery (Chapter 1), and a person without a tribe could not easily protect life or property (Chapter 8). Discuss how laws, schools and communities protect vulnerable people today.

themes.title: Fair trade and debt:
themes.description: Usury made the rich richer and the poor poorer (Chapters 6–7), and the Qur’an forbade usury and allowed only honest trade (Chapter 12). Connect this with fair prices, honest trade and responsible borrowing.

themes.title: Agreements that make travel safe:
themes.description: Trade agreements and the sacred months made travel and trade safer (Chapter 5). Compare them with agreements and rules that protect travelers and traders today.

themes.title: The equal worth of every person:
themes.description: Chapter 15 says that background, wealth, gender and social power do not make one person more valuable than another. Connect this with non-discrimination at school and online.

actions: Write three class rules that protect a student who has no one to stand up for them.
Find out how one charity or aid organization in your area helps people in poverty or debt, and write two sentences about it.
Check one school activity or notice: Can every student take part, whatever their background or money? Suggest one change if not.

exitTicket: One idea from today’s chapter, with the sentence that supports it, is …
One language pattern I noticed today, and what it does in the sentence, is …
One fair action I can take this week that connects with the chapter is …

miniProject.title: Then and Now: A Fairer Community
miniProject.desc: In groups, choose one problem the book describes (weak protection, usury and debt, tribal pressure, or the unequal treatment of women and slaves). Make a one-page poster or a two-minute audio report in clear English: Quote one sentence from the book, explain it in your own words, and describe how people or institutions try to solve a similar problem today. Use at least three Language Focus patterns, such as “because of …”, “while …”, “prevent … from …” or “so … that …”.

reflectivePrompt.title: Every Person Is Important
reflectivePrompt.desc: The last chapter says that background, wealth, gender and social power do not make one person more valuable than another. Write six to eight sentences about a situation at school or in your community where someone was treated fairly — or unfairly — because of money, family or status. What happened, how did people react, and what would a fair response look like?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Require source evidence first, then connect a supported value to an age-appropriate observable action. Do not turn value reflection into a new historical or religious claim. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D14 Respect
items.value: Respect appears through dignity, non-discrimination, protection of rights and disagreement without coercion.

items.label: D5 Sensitivity
items.value: Sensitivity is connected with noticing poverty, debt, slavery, exclusion, hunger and unequal protection.

items.label: D6 Honesty
items.value: Honesty includes accurate definition, careful quantifiers, source attribution and refusal of overgeneralization.

items.label: D16 Responsibility
items.value: Responsibility appears in fair use of power, wealth, rules and community roles.

items.label: D20 Helpfulness / D9 Compassion
items.value: Helpfulness and compassion are expressed through solidarity with vulnerable people and rejection of collective harm.

questions: What observable action could show the same value today?
Which part is source evidence and which part is your own application?

test.title: End-of-Level Test B1
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the B1 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 70 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.

professionalDevelopment.intro: Use these steps to plan your own development with this book: rate yourself on the EPG areas with this book’s chapters, let a colleague observe one of two lessons, keep a short log after each chapter, run one small classroom enquiry, work with colleagues, and agree on scoring before the End-of-Level Test.

peerObservation.focus: Explain three conditions that made Mecca a busy trading city: Its location, the trade agreements of Hashim and the Quraysh leaders, and the sacred months.

content.chapter: Chapter 1: The City and the Age
objectives: I can explain why the period before Islam was called the Jahiliyyah.
I can describe who held power in Mecca and who suffered.

content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Decide what “this reason” refers to, choose because or while to give a reason or a contrast, then rewrite two sentences: one that keeps the focus on the people affected (others often treated them badly) and one that reports a source (In the Qur’an, this period is described as …).
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: JA-hi-LIY-yah, CHA-ot-ic, MIS-er-y, CRU-el-ty. Pause after the reason: “For this reason, / the city was known as the Republic of Merchants.”
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, look at the two hotspots. What do you think a “Republic of Merchants” is? Listen once for the main idea: What was life like before Islam? Read paragraph 2 again and mark who had power and who lived in misery.
discussionPoints: The chapter says poor and weak people lived in misery while powerful people controlled life. Where can you see a power gap today, and what could make it fairer?

content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Decide what “had not been discovered yet” says about the order of events, change a so-result into a because-reason and a noun (the discovery) into a clause, then choose where, to build and grow.

metadata.title: Mecca B1 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 25 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B1 learners who study Mecca Before Islam on their own or at home.
learningGoals: Understand the 15 chapters of Mecca Before Islam.
Find evidence in the story before answering.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
Connect justice, mercy and fairness with real actions.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Listen and read before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 15.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One person in the book I want to remember, and why:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 15 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1: A clear plan helps you keep going and see your progress.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
If you like, choose a weekly goal in your Seyahatname. A new week starts on Monday.
Write one personal goal for this book, for example a skill you want to improve.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week. Short, spaced reviews help you remember.
Before Chapter 1, answer the “I can” statements in section 10, “Look Back”. Answer them again when you finish.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 25 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and hotspots.
Listen and read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Listen and Read
sections.text: Use the audio twice: Once for the main idea, once to follow the exact words.
points: First listening: What is the chapter about?
Second listening: Follow the text line by line.
Replay one long sentence and say it with the same pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes and Hotspots
sections.text: Each chapter has five Word Notes and two picture hotspots. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has four Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and its meaning.
Activities 2–3 (Build): choose, rewrite or correct forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say five to six connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Work one paragraph at a time.
Use the hotspots to get the big picture first.
Write a one-line summary of each paragraph.
Focus on two Word Notes today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Story
sections.text: The book contrasts the Jahiliyyah with justice and mercy. Connect each value to one action.
points: Fairness: Honest trade instead of usury (Chapters 6, 7, 12).
Protection of the weak: Support people without powerful friends (Chapter 13).
Right loyalty: Do not follow a group when it is wrong (Chapter 8).
Equal worth: background, wealth and gender do not decide a person’s value (Chapter 15).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 15, do the review pages in this order. Go back to the chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Master Glossary
Places & People
Vocabulary Challenge
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back: My Level and My Learning
sections.text: Answer these statements before Chapter 1 and again after the Final Challenge: not yet, partly or yes. They come from the CEFR Companion Volume (Council of Europe, 2020) for level B1. One book is one step towards them, not a test.
points: Reading: “I can follow the plot of stories, simple novels and comics with a clear linear storyline and high frequency everyday language, given regular use of a dictionary.”
Speaking: “I can relate the plot of a book or film and describe my reactions.”
Writing: “I can produce straightforward connected text on topics that are familiar or of personal interest.”
Mediation: “I can convey information given in clear, well-structured informational texts on subjects that are familiar or of personal or current interest.”
Which study steps helped me most in this book, and why?
What was hard, and which strategy did I use?
What will I change in my plan for the next book?
